claim: PRDM9 deposits H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 at future double-strand break (DSB) sites during the very early stages of meiosis.
source: The histone modification writer Prdm9 has been shown to deposit H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 at future double-strand break (DSB) sites during the very early stages of meiosis, but the reader of these marks remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing PRDM9's histone modification activity.

claim: ZCWPW1 is an H3K4me3 reader that is required for DSB repair and synapsis in mouse testes.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Zcwpw1 is an H3K4me3 reader that is required for DSB repair and synapsis in mouse testes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from H3K4me3 reader-dead mutant mice and ChIP-seq analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: H3K4me3 reader-dead Zcwpw1 mutant mice have spermatocytes arrested at the pachytene-like stage.
source: We generated H3K4me3 reader-dead Zcwpw1 mutant mice and found that their spermatocytes were arrested at the pachytene-like stage, which phenocopies the Zcwpw1 knock–out mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and immunofluorescence data comparing WT, Zcwpw1−/−, and Zcwpw1KI/KI mice.

claim: ZCWPW1's occupancy on chromatin is strongly promoted by the histone-modification activity of PRDM9.
source: Based on various ChIP-seq and immunofluorescence analyses using several mutants, we found that Zcwpw1's occupancy on chromatin is strongly promoted by the histone-modification activity of PRDM9.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data comparing WT and Prdm9−/− mice showing loss of ZCWPW1 peaks in the absence of PRDM9.

claim: ZCWPW1 localizes to DMC1-labelled hotspots in a largely Prdm9-dependent manner.
source: Zcwpw1 localizes to DMC1-labelled hotspots in a largely Prdm9-dependent manner, where it facilitates completion of synapsis by mediating the DSB repair process.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing overlap between ZCWPW1 peaks and DMC1 peaks, and loss of ZCWPW1 at these sites in Prdm9−/− mice.

claim: ZCWPW1 facilitates completion of synapsis by mediating the DSB repair process.
source: Zcwpw1 localizes to DMC1-labelled hotspots in a largely Prdm9-dependent manner, where it facilitates completion of synapsis by mediating the DSB repair process.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing incomplete synapsis and persistent DSB markers in Zcwpw1 mutant mice.

claim: ZCWPW1 functions as part of the selection system for epigenetics-based recombination hotspots in mammals.
source: In sum, our study demonstrates the function of ZCWPW1 that acts as part of the selection system for epigenetics-based recombination hotspots in mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of multiple experimental findings showing ZCWPW1's role in reading PRDM9-deposited marks at recombination hotspots.

claim: Meiotic recombination ensures the faithful transmission of the genome through the pairing and segregation of homologous chromosomes.
source: Meiotic recombination ensures the faithful transmission of the genome through the pairing and segregation of homologous chromosomes, and it increases genetic diversity by disrupting linkage relationships (Bolcun-Filas and Schimenti, 2012; Handel and Schimenti, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on meiotic recombination.

claim: Meiotic recombination increases genetic diversity by disrupting linkage relationships.
source: Meiotic recombination ensures the faithful transmission of the genome through the pairing and segregation of homologous chromosomes, and it increases genetic diversity by disrupting linkage relationships (Bolcun-Filas and Schimenti, 2012; Handel and Schimenti, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on meiotic recombination.

claim: Meiotic recombination is initiated by the induction of programmed DSBs that are repaired by homologous recombination.
source: At the molecular level, meiotic recombination is initiated by the induction of programmed DSBs that are repaired by homologous recombination, leading to gene conversion and cross over formation (Gray and Cohen, 2016; Hunter, 2015; Zickler and Kleckner, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on the molecular mechanisms of meiotic recombination.

claim: DSB locations are marked at the very earliest stages of meiosis by trimethylation of histone H3 on lysine 4 (H3K4me3).
source: DSB induction is a complex process, and DSB locations are known to be marked at the very earliest stages of meiosis by trimethylation of histone H3 on lysine 4 (H3K4me3) (Baudat et al., 2013; de Massy, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing the role of H3K4me3 in marking DSB sites.

claim: In mammals, H3K4me3 marking at DSB sites is performed by the protein PRDM9.
source: In mammals, this is performed by the protein PRDM9, which is expressed in the leptotene and zygotene substages (Parvanov et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on PRDM9 function.

claim: PRDM9 is expressed in the leptotene and zygotene substages.
source: In mammals, this is performed by the protein PRDM9, which is expressed in the leptotene and zygotene substages (Parvanov et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on PRDM9 expression patterns.

claim: PRDM9 is a DNA-binding zinc finger protein with an exceptionally long and genetically variable zinc finger domain that determines its binding specificity.
source: PRDM9 is a DNA-binding zinc finger protein, with an exceptionally long and genetically variable zinc finger domain that determines its binding specificity (for defining recombination hotspots), while its SET domain possesses histone trimethyl transferase activity, and its KRAB domain is involved in protein–protein interactions (Grey et al., 2018; Paigen and Petkov, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work characterizing PRDM9 structure and function.

claim: PRDM9's SET domain possesses histone trimethyl transferase activity.
source: PRDM9 is a DNA-binding zinc finger protein, with an exceptionally long and genetically variable zinc finger domain that determines its binding specificity (for defining recombination hotspots), while its SET domain possesses histone trimethyl transferase activity, and its KRAB domain is involved in protein–protein interactions (Grey et al., 2018; Paigen and Petkov, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work characterizing PRDM9 enzymatic activity.

claim: PRDM9's KRAB domain is involved in protein–protein interactions.
source: PRDM9 is a DNA-binding zinc finger protein, with an exceptionally long and genetically variable zinc finger domain that determines its binding specificity (for defining recombination hotspots), while its SET domain possesses histone trimethyl transferase activity, and its KRAB domain is involved in protein–protein interactions (Grey et al., 2018; Paigen and Petkov, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work characterizing PRDM9 domains.

claim: In yeast, the histone reader Spp1 links H3K4me3 sites at promoters with the DSB formation machinery, thus promoting DSB formation.
source: In yeast, the histone reader Spp1 links H3K4me3 sites at promoters with the DSB formation machinery, thus promoting DSB formation (Acquaviva et al., 2013; Sommermeyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on Spp1 function in yeast.

claim: In mice, the H3K4me3 writer Prdm9 controls the locations of DSB formation.
source: In mice, although multiple studies have shown that the H3K4me3 writer Prdm9 controls the locations of DSB formation (Baudat et al., 2010; Brick et al., 2012; Diagouraga et al., 2018; Grey et al., 2017; Myers et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010; Powers et al., 2016), much less is known about the subsequent activities of any proteins that might read these epigenetic marks and thus participate in advancing the meiotic recombination process (Paigen and Petkov, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies on PRDM9 function in mice.

claim: DSB formation at sites defined by PRDM9 is catalyzed by an evolutionarily conserved topoisomerase-like enzyme complex consisting of the SPO11 enzyme and its binding partner TOPOVIBL.
source: DSB formation at sites defined by PRDM9 is catalyzed by an evolutionarily conserved topoisomerase-like enzyme complex consisting of the SPO11 enzyme and its binding partner TOPOVIBL (Bergerat et al., 1997; Keeney et al., 1997; Panizza et al., 2011; Robert et al., 2016; Vrielynck et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the SPO11 complex.

claim: SPO11-mediated cleavage results in single-strand DNA overhangs that are subsequently coated by various proteins, including DMC1 and RAD51.
source: SPO11-mediated cleavage results in single-strand DNA overhangs that are subsequently coated by various proteins, including DMC1 and RAD51 (Dai et al., 2017; Pittman et al., 1998; Tarsounas et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on DSB processing.

claim: DSBs enable homology searching and alignment to occur, which in turn promote homology synapsis and DSB repair.
source: The DSBs enable homology searching and alignment to occur, which in turn promote homology synapsis and DSB repair (Inagaki et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on DSB-mediated homology interactions.

claim: DSB-mediated interactions and repair processes occur differentially between homologous nonsister chromatids, rather than between sisters, as occurs in mitotic DSB repair.
source: A basic feature of meiosis is that DSB-mediated interactions and repair processes occur differentially between homologous nonsister chromatids, rather than between sisters, as occurs in mitotic DSB repair (Garcia et al., 2015; Keeney et al., 2014; Lange et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on meiotic vs. mitotic DSB repair.

claim: Some DSBs are repaired in a way that generates crossovers, wherein DNA is exchanged between homologous chromosomes.
source: Some DSBs are repaired in a way that generates crossovers, wherein DNA is exchanged between homologous chromosomes (Baudat and de Massy, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on crossover formation.

claim: The ZMM proteins (e.g., TEX11, MSH4/MSH5, and RNF212) are a group of functionally related proteins known for their roles in promoting the formation of crossovers.
source: The ZMM proteins (e.g., TEX11, MSH4/MSH5, and RNF212) are a group of functionally related proteins known for their roles in promoting the formation of crossovers (Edelmann et al., 1999; Kneitz et al., 2000; Lynn et al., 2007; Reynolds et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on ZMM proteins.

claim: Zcwpw1 protein is required for meiosis prophase I in mice.
source: We previously reported that the zinc finger CW-type and PWWP domain containing 1 (Zcwpw1) protein is required for meiosis prophase I in mice, and we found that Zcwpw1 deficiency disrupted spermatogenesis in male mice but did not disrupt oogenesis in females to the same extent (Li et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Zcwpw1 deficiency disrupted spermatogenesis in male mice but did not disrupt oogenesis in females to the same extent.
source: We previously reported that the zinc finger CW-type and PWWP domain containing 1 (Zcwpw1) protein is required for meiosis prophase I in mice, and we found that Zcwpw1 deficiency disrupted spermatogenesis in male mice but did not disrupt oogenesis in females to the same extent (Li et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Zcwpw1 is a member of the CW-domain containing protein family.
source: Zcwpw1 is a member of the CW-domain containing protein family (Liu et al., 2016; Perry, 2003), and its zinc finger CW (zf-CW) domain has three conserved tryptophan and four conserved cysteine residues.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on CW-domain proteins.

claim: The zinc finger CW (zf-CW) domain of ZCWPW1 has three conserved tryptophan and four conserved cysteine residues.
source: Zcwpw1 is a member of the CW-domain containing protein family (Liu et al., 2016; Perry, 2003), and its zinc finger CW (zf-CW) domain has three conserved tryptophan and four conserved cysteine residues.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents established knowledge about the zf-CW domain structure.

claim: Structural analysis has shown that human ZCWPW1 zf-CW domain is a histone modification reader.
source: Structural analysis has shown that human ZCWPW1 zf-CW domain is a histone modification reader (He et al., 2010), while chromatin pulldown analysis has confirmed that ZCWPW1 zf-CW domain recognizes H3K4me3 marks (Hoppmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior structural work.

claim: Chromatin pulldown analysis has confirmed that ZCWPW1 zf-CW domain recognizes H3K4me3 marks.
source: Structural analysis has shown that human ZCWPW1 zf-CW domain is a histone modification reader (He et al., 2010), while chromatin pulldown analysis has confirmed that ZCWPW1 zf-CW domain recognizes H3K4me3 marks (Hoppmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior biochemical work.

claim: Four amino acids – W256, E301, T302, and W303 – are primarily responsible for the binding of ZCWPW1 zf-CW domain to H3K4me3 marks in humans.
source: A crystal structure of the human zf-CW domain of ZCWPW1 in complex with a peptide bearing an H3K4me3 mark revealed that four amino acids – W256, E301, T302, and W303 – are primarily responsible for the binding of ZCWPW1 zf-CW domain to H3K4me3 marks (He et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior structural work.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed the absence of the ZCWPW1 protein in Zcwpw1−/− testes.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed the absence of the ZCWPW1 protein in Zcwpw1−/− testes, while the Zcwpw1W247I/E292R/W294P variant protein was expressed at a level similar to that of the wild type (WT) protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The Zcwpw1W247I/E292R/W294P variant protein was expressed at a level similar to that of the wild type (WT) protein.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed the absence of the ZCWPW1 protein in Zcwpw1−/− testes, while the Zcwpw1W247I/E292R/W294P variant protein was expressed at a level similar to that of the wild type (WT) protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining revealed that the ZCWPW1 protein was undetectable in Zcwpw1−/− spermatocytes but could still be found in Zcwpw1W247I/E292R/W294P mutant spermatocytes.
source: Consistent with the western blot data, immunofluorescence staining of frozen sections from 8-week-old WT, Zcwpw1−/−, and Zcwpw1KI/KI mouse testes revealed that the ZCWPW1 protein was undetectable in Zcwpw1−/− spermatocytes but could still be found in Zcwpw1W247I/E292R/W294P mutant spermatocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Hematoxylin staining showed that spermatogenesis was disrupted in both the Zcwpw1−/− and Zcwpw1KI/KI mice.
source: Hematoxylin staining showed that spermatogenesis was disrupted in both the Zcwpw1−/− and Zcwpw1KI/KI mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The seminiferous tubules of the Zcwpw1-/- and Zcwpw1KI/KI mice lacked post-meiotic cell types, contained apoptotic cells, or were nearly empty.
source: Compared with the WT mice, the seminiferous tubules of the Zcwpw1-/- and Zcwpw1KI/KI mice lacked post-meiotic cell types, contained apoptotic cells, or were nearly empty.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There were no obvious sperm detected in either the Zcwpw1−/− or Zcwpw1KI/KI epididymides.
source: Furthermore, the WT epididymides were full of sperm, but there were no obvious sperm detected in either the Zcwpw1−/− or Zcwpw1KI/KI samples, suggesting meiotic arrest in these mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Immunostaining of SYCP1 and SYCP3 showed no differences among any of the genotypes with regard to leptotene-to-zygotene progression.
source: Immunostaining of SYCP1 and SYCP3 showed no differences among any of the genotypes with regard to leptotene-to-zygotene progression, which appeared normal in all mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Among 164 spermatocytes in Zcwpw1−/− testes and 158 spermatocytes in Zcwpw1KI/KI testes none had complete synapsis.
source: In contrast, among 164 spermatocytes in Zcwpw1−/− testes and 158 spermatocytes in Zcwpw1KI/KI testes none had complete synapsis, and we only detected around of 8 synapsed chromosome pairs in Zcwpw1−/− and Zcwpw1KI/KI spermatocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D; Li et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of synapsis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Around 8 synapsed chromosome pairs were detected in Zcwpw1−/− and Zcwpw1KI/KI spermatocytes.
source: In contrast, among 164 spermatocytes in Zcwpw1−/− testes and 158 spermatocytes in Zcwpw1KI/KI testes none had complete synapsis, and we only detected around of 8 synapsed chromosome pairs in Zcwpw1−/− and Zcwpw1KI/KI spermatocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D; Li et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of synapsis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Spermatocytes lacking the H3K4me3-reader activity of the Zcwpw1 protein have severely disrupted synapsis.
source: Thus, spermatocytes lacking the H3K4me3-reader activity of the Zcwpw1 protein have severely disrupted synapsis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the synapsis defects observed in Zcwpw1KI/KI mice.

claim: There were no differences in the numbers of DMC1 or RAD51 foci in the leptotene or zygotene stages between WT and Zcwpw1KI/KI mice.
source: There were no differences in the numbers of DMC1 or RAD51 foci in the leptotene or zygotene stages of the two genotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C and E.

claim: Zcwpw1KI/KI pachytene-like spermatocytes retained a large number of DMC1 and RAD51 foci.
source: However, analysis of WT pachytene and Zcwpw1KI/KI pachytene-like spermatocytes revealed an obvious discrepancy. Decreased numbers of DMC1 and RAD51 foci were seen in the pachytene WT spermatocytes, indicating successful repair of DSBs, but the Zcwpw1KI/KI pachytene-like spermatocytes retained a large number of DMC1 and RAD51 foci (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C, D, E, and F.

claim: The repair of DSBs is disrupted in the absence of a functional ZCWPW1 H3K4me3 reader protein.
source: These results suggest that the repair of DSBs is disrupted in the absence of a functional ZCWPW1 H3K4me3 reader protein and that Zcwpw1 might facilitate meiotic DSB repair downstream of strand invasion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the persistence of DMC1 and RAD51 foci in Zcwpw1KI/KI spermatocytes.

claim: Zcwpw1 might facilitate meiotic DSB repair downstream of strand invasion.
source: These results suggest that the repair of DSBs is disrupted in the absence of a functional ZCWPW1 H3K4me3 reader protein and that Zcwpw1 might facilitate meiotic DSB repair downstream of strand invasion.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed persistence of recombination factors.

claim: MSH4 and RNF212 signals decreased as expected in WT pachytene spermatocytes, but persisted on the pachytene-like Zcwpw1KI/KI chromosomes.
source: Staining for MSH4 and RNF212 showed that the recombination machinery could assemble normally in both WT and Zcwpw1KI/KI spermatocytes at the zygotene stage. However, these MSH4 and RNF212 signals decreased as expected in WT pachytene spermatocytes, but persisted on the pachytene-like Zcwpw1KI/KI chromosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B, C, and D.

claim: The recombination process was arrested in the pachytene-like spermatocytes lacking Zcwpw1 H3K4me3-reader function.
source: Additionally, the MLH1 staining patterns indicated that Holliday junction resolution proceeded normally in mid- to late-pachytene WT spermatocytes but indicated that the recombination process was arrested in the pachytene-like spermatocytes lacking Zcwpw1 H3K4me3-reader function, which failed to progress to the pachytene stage and for which no crossover occurred, thus resulting in the absence of MLH1 foci (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: No crossover occurred in pachytene-like spermatocytes lacking Zcwpw1 H3K4me3-reader function.
source: Additionally, the MLH1 staining patterns indicated that Holliday junction resolution proceeded normally in mid- to late-pachytene WT spermatocytes but indicated that the recombination process was arrested in the pachytene-like spermatocytes lacking Zcwpw1 H3K4me3-reader function, which failed to progress to the pachytene stage and for which no crossover occurred, thus resulting in the absence of MLH1 foci (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of MLH1 foci in Zcwpw1KI/KI spermatocytes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Both DSB repair and recombination are defective in the Zcwpw1KI/KI mice.
source: These results suggest that both DSB repair and recombination are defective in the Zcwpw1KI/KI mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of persistent DSB markers and absence of crossover markers.

claim: DSBs could form normally in all of the genotypes (WT, Zcwpw1−/−, and Zcwpw1KI/KI).
source: We found that DSBs could form normally in all of the genotypes (Figure 2A), but there were obvious differences between pachytene WT spermatocytes and pachytene-like Zcwpw1−/− and Zcwpw1KI/KI spermatocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by γH2AX staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: WT pachytene spermatocytes exhibited no obvious signal for γH2AX on autosomes, but retained a γH2AX signal on the sex chromosomes.
source: The WT pachytene spermatocytes exhibited no obvious signal for γH2AX on autosomes, but retained a γH2AX signal on the sex chromosomes, which corresponds to the XY sex body and indicates silencing of the sex chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by γH2AX staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both autosomes and sex chromosomes retained obvious γH2AX signals in Zcwpw1−/− or Zcwpw1KI/KI pachytene-like spermatocytes.
source: In contrast, both autosomes and sex chromosomes retained obvious γH2AX signals, and no XY bodies were observed in Zcwpw1−/− or Zcwpw1KI/KI pachytene-like spermatocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by γH2AX staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No XY bodies were observed in Zcwpw1−/− or Zcwpw1KI/KI pachytene-like spermatocytes.
source: In contrast, both autosomes and sex chromosomes retained obvious γH2AX signals, and no XY bodies were observed in Zcwpw1−/− or Zcwpw1KI/KI pachytene-like spermatocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by γH2AX staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both autosomes and sex chromosomes retained obvious p-ATM signals in the pachytene-like Zcwpw1−/− and Zcwpw1KI/KI spermatocytes.
source: We next stained against the DSB-repair machinery component p-ATM and found that both autosomes and sex chromosomes retained obvious p-ATM signals in the pachytene-like Zcwpw1−/− and Zcwpw1KI/KI spermatocytes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by p-ATM staining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Wells et al. found that DSBs occur in the same hotspot regions in Zcwpw1−/−male mice through single−stranded DNA sequencing (SSDS) by ChIP-seq against DMC1.
source: Through single−stranded DNA sequencing (SSDS) by ChIP-seq against DMC1, Wells et al. found that DSBs occur in the same hotspot regions in Zcwpw1−/−male mice (Mahgoub et al., 2019; Wells et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work by Wells et al. and Mahgoub et al.

claim: Mahgoub et al. confirmed that DSBs in both WT and Zcwpw1−/−mice completely overlapped with each other and with previously identified hotpots using quantitative END−seq.
source: Similarly, using quantitative END−seq, Mahgoub et al. also confirmed that DSBs in both WT and Zcwpw1−/−mice completely overlapped with each other and with previously identified hotpots (Mahgoub et al., 2019; Wells et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work by Mahgoub et al.

claim: Zcwpw1 is dispensable for the induction and location of DSBs.
source: These results indicate that Zcwpw1 is dispensable for the induction and location of DSBs but is required for proper interhomolog interactions, including synapsis and the repair of DSBs that occur during the later steps of homologous recombination.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that DSBs form normally in Zcwpw1 mutants and is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Zcwpw1 is required for proper interhomolog interactions, including synapsis and the repair of DSBs that occur during the later steps of homologous recombination.
source: These results indicate that Zcwpw1 is dispensable for the induction and location of DSBs but is required for proper interhomolog interactions, including synapsis and the repair of DSBs that occur during the later steps of homologous recombination.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of normal DSB formation but defective synapsis and repair in Zcwpw1 mutants.

claim: The Zcwpw1 ChIP-seq data for C57BL/6 mouse testis chromatin revealed a total of 14,688 Zcwpw1 peaks.
source: The Zcwpw1 ChIP-seq data for C57BL/6 mouse testis chromatin revealed a total of 14,688 Zcwpw1 peaks, with 499 peaks localized within 2,000 bp upstream of a transcription start site (TSS), 2146 peaks localized in exons, 6172 peaks localized in introns, and 5871 peaks localized within intergenic regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 11.5% of the ZCWPW1 binding sites overlapped with promoters.
source: Among all ZCWPW1 binding sites detected in mouse testes, 11.5% of the ZCWPW1 binding sites (peaks) overlapped with promoters, while 6.1% of ZCWPW1 binding sites overlapped with CpG islands (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 6.1% of ZCWPW1 binding sites overlapped with CpG islands.
source: Among all ZCWPW1 binding sites detected in mouse testes, 11.5% of the ZCWPW1 binding sites (peaks) overlapped with promoters, while 6.1% of ZCWPW1 binding sites overlapped with CpG islands (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ZCWPW1 binding sites were not significantly enriched in the transposable element regions compared with random binding sites.
source: Compared with the random binding sites, ZCWPW1 binding sites were not significantly enriched in the transposable element regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Analysis of RNA-seq data of postnatal day 14 (PD14) WT and Zcwpw1−/− mice identified 567 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), including 464 downregulated and 103 upregulated DEGs in Zcwpw1−/− testes compared with WT testes.
source: Analysis of RNA-seq data of postnatal day 14 (PD14) WT and Zcwpw1−/− mice identified 567 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), including 464 downregulated and 103 upregulated DEGs in Zcwpw1−/− testes compared with WT testes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The down-regulated genes in Zcwpw1−/− testes were enriched in axoneme assembly, male gamete generation and flagellated sperm motility.
source: Gene ontology analysis showed that the down-regulated genes were enriched in axoneme assembly, male gamete generation and flagellated sperm motility (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Most of the DEGs were not the genes whose promoters overlapped with ZCWPW1 binding sites.
source: However, most of the DEGs were not the genes whose promoters overlapped with ZCWPW1 binding sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: ZCWPW1 may not affect the transcription level of many genes sharing promoter overlap with ZCWPW1.
source: These results strongly suggest that ZCWPW1 may not affect the transcription level of many genes sharing promoter overlap with ZCWPW1, even though Zcwpw1−/− (vs WT) spermatocytes have two up-regulated genes and 45 down-regulated genes with such promoter overlap (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the limited overlap between DEGs and genes with ZCWPW1-bound promoters.

claim: The H3K4me3 ChIP-seq data in C57BL/6 mice revealed a total of 55,801 H3K4me3 peaks.
source: The H3K4me3 ChIP-seq data in C57BL/6 mice revealed a total of 55,801 H3K4me3 peaks, consistent with a previous report of 55,497 H3K4me3 peaks in whole testes (Smagulova et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis and is consistent with prior work.

claim: Lam et al. detected a total of 75,771 H3K4me3 peaks among isolated SCP3+H1T− spermatocytes.
source: Lam et al. described a method for isolating pure sub-populations of meiotic substage nuclei, and they detected a total of 75,771 H3K4me3 peaks among isolated SCP3+H1T− spermatocytes; this signature defines pre-leptotene to early-pachytene substage spermatocytes (Lam et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by Lam et al.

claim: 97.8% (14,369 of 14,688 peaks) of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with the H3K4me3 peaks reported by Lam et al.
source: In light of the known capacity of Zcwpw1 to recognize epigenetic methylation modification marks, we compared the ZCWPW1 peaks with these two sets of H3K4me3 peaks, and we found that 97.8% (14,369 of 14,688 peaks) of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with the H3K4me3 peaks reported by Lam et al, while 39.4% (5,792 of 14,688 peaks) of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with the H3K4me3 peaks in our data (Figure 3A and B), therefore supporting the hypothesis that this specific overlap with H3K4me3 peaks serves as a means for Zcwpw1 recognition of histone modification marks.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: 39.4% (5,792 of 14,688 peaks) of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with the H3K4me3 peaks in our data.
source: In light of the known capacity of Zcwpw1 to recognize epigenetic methylation modification marks, we compared the ZCWPW1 peaks with these two sets of H3K4me3 peaks, and we found that 97.8% (14,369 of 14,688 peaks) of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with the H3K4me3 peaks reported by Lam et al, while 39.4% (5,792 of 14,688 peaks) of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with the H3K4me3 peaks in our data (Figure 3A and B), therefore supporting the hypothesis that this specific overlap with H3K4me3 peaks serves as a means for Zcwpw1 recognition of histone modification marks.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: No Zcwpw1 peaks were detected in the Zcwpw1−/− or Zcwpw1KI/KI mice.
source: The analysis indicated that no Zcwpw1 peaks were detected in the Zcwpw1−/− or Zcwpw1KI/KI mice (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3A and D.

claim: The H3K4me3 reader function of ZCWPW1 is essential for its ability to bind to chromatin and to function in meiosis prophase I in male mice.
source: These in vivo results, viewed alongside the previous reports of Zcwpw1 function in the meiotic process demonstrating that these specific mutations in the ZCWPW1 zf-CW domain affect the protein's ability to read histone modifications (including H3K4me3), together indicate that the Zcwpw1W247I/E292R/W294P mutant is an H3K4me3 reader-dead variant of Zcwpw1. Furthermore, these results suggest that the H3K4me3 reader function of this protein is essential for its ability to bind to chromatin and to function in meiosis prophase I in male mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations that the reader-dead mutant cannot bind chromatin and phenocopies the knockout.

claim: 90.1% of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with the H3K36me3 peaks reported by Lam et al. in isolated stage-specific spermatocyte nuclei.
source: We found that 90.1% of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with the H3K36me3 peaks reported by Lam et al. in isolated stage-specific spermatocyte nuclei, while 24.8% of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with the H3K36me3 peaks identified by Grey et al. in whole testes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 24.8% of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with the H3K36me3 peaks identified by Grey et al. in whole testes.
source: We found that 90.1% of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with the H3K36me3 peaks reported by Lam et al. in isolated stage-specific spermatocyte nuclei, while 24.8% of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with the H3K36me3 peaks identified by Grey et al. in whole testes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 88.8% of the ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with regions containing both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks.
source: In analyzing the correlation between ZCWPW1 binding sites and these two histone modification marks, we found that 88.8% of the ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with regions containing both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks, while only 9.1% and 1.3% of ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 peaks individually (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Only 9.1% and 1.3% of ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 peaks individually.
source: In analyzing the correlation between ZCWPW1 binding sites and these two histone modification marks, we found that 88.8% of the ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with regions containing both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks, while only 9.1% and 1.3% of ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 peaks individually (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The ZCWPW1 peak intensity was significantly higher for the dual overlapping regions than for regions containing either H3K4me3 or H3K36me3 alone.
source: Furthermore, the ZCWPW1 peak intensity was significantly higher for the dual overlapping regions than for regions containing either H3K4me3 or H3K36me3 alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq peak intensity analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: ZCWPW1 bound H3K4me3 regions had higher H3K36me3 levels than H3K4me3 regions were not bound by ZCWPW1.
source: We also found that ZCWPW1 bound H3K4me3 regions had higher H3K36me3 levels than H3K4me3 regions were not bound by ZCWPW1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq signal analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The pattern for both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 signals were similar to the Zcwpw1 expression pattern in the leptotene and zygotene stages.
source: We conducted immunofluorescence analysis of chromosome spreads of spermatocytes from adult mice using rat anti-ZCWPW1 and rabbit anti-H3K4me3/H3K36me3 antibodies and found, consistent with the ChIP-seq data, that the pattern for both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 signals were similar to the Zcwpw1 expression pattern we observed in the leptotene and zygotene stages (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: Mahgoub et al., 2019 confirmed that recombinant ZCWPW1 (1–440aa) binds with the highest affinity to H3K4me3/K36me3 peptides in vitro.
source: Moreover, Mahgoub et al., 2019 confirmed that recombinant ZCWPW1 (1–440aa) binds with the highest affinity to H3K4me3/K36me3 peptides in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work by Mahgoub et al.

claim: ZCWPW1 preferentially binds to sites with both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that ZCWPW1 preferentially binds to sites with both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined ChIP-seq and biochemical data showing preferential binding to dual-marked regions.

claim: A de novo motif identified within the Zcwpw1 binding sites is highly correlated with a known Prdm9 binding motif in mice.
source: This analysis identified a de novo motif that is highly correlated with a known Prdm9 binding motif in mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; Billings et al., 2013; Ségurel, 2013; Walker et al., 2015), and this suggested that Zcwpw1 binding to chromatin might occur in a Prdm9-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: 13% of the Zcwpw1 peaks obtained in our study overlapped with Grey et al.'s in vivo Prdm9 peaks.
source: At the genome-wide level, 13% of the Zcwpw1 peaks obtained in our study overlapped with Grey et al.'s in vivo Prdm9 peaks, while 74% of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with Walker et al.'s in vitro Prdm9 peaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis comparing with published PRDM9 data.

claim: 74% of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with Walker et al.'s in vitro Prdm9 peaks.
source: At the genome-wide level, 13% of the Zcwpw1 peaks obtained in our study overlapped with Grey et al.'s in vivo Prdm9 peaks, while 74% of the Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with Walker et al.'s in vitro Prdm9 peaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis comparing with published PRDM9 data.

claim: 99.5% of the ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with PRDM9 in Grey et al are covered by that ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with PRDM9 peaks in Walker et al.
source: Moreover, it should be noted that 99.5% of the ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with PRDM9 in Grey et al are covered by that ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with PRDM9 peaks in Walker et al (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: 1934 of 2,601 Prdm9 peaks (74%) from Grey et al. overlapped with our Zcwpw1 peaks.
source: Conversely, we found that 1934 of 2,601 Prdm9 peaks (74%) from Grey et al. and 10,975 of 36,898 PRDM9 peaks (29.7%) from Walker et al. overlapped with our Zcwpw1 peaks (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: 10,975 of 36,898 PRDM9 peaks (29.7%) from Walker et al. overlapped with our Zcwpw1 peaks.
source: Conversely, we found that 1934 of 2,601 Prdm9 peaks (74%) from Grey et al. and 10,975 of 36,898 PRDM9 peaks (29.7%) from Walker et al. overlapped with our Zcwpw1 peaks (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The majority of PRDM9-dependent H3K4me3 peaks disappeared in Prdm9−/− mice.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Brick et al., 2012), the majority of PRDM9-dependent H3K4me3 peaks disappeared in Prdm9−/− mice (Figure 4D and E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data comparing WT and Prdm9−/− mice shown in Figure 4D and E, and is consistent with prior work.

claim: 94.7% loss in Zcwpw1 binding sites was observed in Prdm9−/− testes compared to WT.
source: In our ChIP-seq data, we found that the H3K4me3 peaks overlapped with Prdm9 binding sites (Grey et al., 2017); with the notable exception of a 94.7% loss in Zcwpw1 binding sites, we found no obvious discrepancies between WT and Prdm9−/− testes (Figure 4E right panel, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data comparing WT and Prdm9−/− mice shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Zcwpw1 binding is strongly promoted by the specific activity of Prdm9.
source: This suggested that Zcwpw1 binding is strongly promoted by the specific activity of Prdm9 (Figure 4D and E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the loss of ZCWPW1 peaks in Prdm9−/− mice.

claim: 781 ZCWPW1 peaks were maintained in Prdm9−/− mice.
source: We found that although 94.7% of the ZCWPW1 peaks were apparently lost in Prdm9−/− mutant testes, 781 ZCWPW1 peaks were maintained and were accompanied by 652 newly generated ZCWPW1 peaks in Prdm9−/− mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 652 newly generated ZCWPW1 peaks were observed in Prdm9−/− mice.
source: We found that although 94.7% of the ZCWPW1 peaks were apparently lost in Prdm9−/− mutant testes, 781 ZCWPW1 peaks were maintained and were accompanied by 652 newly generated ZCWPW1 peaks in Prdm9−/− mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The new ZCWPW1 peaks were significantly weaker than those of both the maintained and the lost ZCWPW1 peaks in Prdm9−/−mice.
source: Furthermore, examination of peak intensities showed that the new ZCWPW1 peaks were significantly weaker than those of both the maintained and the lost ZCWPW1 peaks in Prdm9−/−mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by peak intensity analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The majority of gained (67.8%) and maintained (83.2%) ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with promoter regions.
source: The majority of these gained (67.8%) and maintained (83.2%) ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with promoter regions, while only 7.4% of the lost ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with promoter regions in Prdm9−/−mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic feature overlap analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Only 7.4% of the lost ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with promoter regions in Prdm9−/−mice.
source: The majority of these gained (67.8%) and maintained (83.2%) ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with promoter regions, while only 7.4% of the lost ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with promoter regions in Prdm9−/−mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic feature overlap analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Nearly 80% of the lost ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with PRDM9 binding sites.
source: Further analysis showed that nearly 80% of the lost ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with PRDM9 binding sites, while the majority of the maintained and gained ZCWPW1 peaks did not overlap with PRDM9 peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: The majority of the maintained and gained ZCWPW1 peaks did not overlap with PRDM9 peaks.
source: Further analysis showed that nearly 80% of the lost ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with PRDM9 binding sites, while the majority of the maintained and gained ZCWPW1 peaks did not overlap with PRDM9 peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: 3,028 ZCWPW1 peaks that were lost and did not overlap with PRDM9 binding sites were significantly enriched at PRDM9 binding sites.
source: Surprisingly, a motif analysis showed that 3,028 ZCWPW1 peaks, i.e., those that were lost and did not overlap with PRDM9 binding sites, were significantly enriched at PRDM9 binding sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F), suggesting that Zcwpw1 binding to these sites is highly Prdm9 dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3F.

claim: 11,124 of the 14,688 total Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with DMC1-defined DSB hotspots.
source: For the WT mice, 11,124 of the 14,688 total Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with DMC1-defined DSB hotspots, while 10,340 of ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with SPO11 oligo-defined DSB hotspots (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 10,340 of ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with SPO11 oligo-defined DSB hotspots.
source: For the WT mice, 11,124 of the 14,688 total Zcwpw1 peaks overlapped with DMC1-defined DSB hotspots, while 10,340 of ZCWPW1 peaks overlapped with SPO11 oligo-defined DSB hotspots (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The greater the ZCWPW1 peak intensity, the better the overlap between the ZCWPW1 peaks and the DMC1 peaks.
source: Specifically, the greater the ZCWPW1 peak intensity, the better the overlap between the ZCWPW1 peaks and the DMC1 peaks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 65.1% of the DMC1 peaks overlapped with both ZCWPW1 binding sites and merged PRDM9 peaks.
source: Further analysis showed that 65.1% of the DMC1 peaks overlapped with both ZCWPW1 binding sites and merged PRDM9 peaks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There was an apparent lack of Zcwpw1 peaks and H3K4me3 signals at DMC1-labelled DSB hotspots in Prdm9−/− mice.
source: Our ZCWPW1 and H3K4me3 ChIP-seq data in WT and Prdm9−/−mice indicated an apparent lack of Zcwpw1 peaks and H3K4me3 signals at DMC1-labelled DSB hotspots (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Occupancy of Zcwpw1 at DMC1-labelled DSB hotspots in Prdm9−/− spermatocytes is largely dependent on Prdm9-mediated histone modifications.
source: These results reinforce the idea that occupancy of Zcwpw1 at DMC1-labelled DSB hotspots in Prdm9−/− spermatocytes is largely dependent on Prdm9-mediated histone modifications.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the loss of ZCWPW1 at DSB hotspots in Prdm9−/− mice.

claim: 781 Zcwpw1 peaks in WT testes did not obviously overlap with DSB hotspots.
source: However, it bears mentioning that we also detected 781 Zcwpw1 peaks in WT testes that did not obviously overlap with DSB hotspots and we detected 652 ZCWPW1 peaks that did not obviously overlap with DSB hotspots in Prdm9−/− mice (Figure 5B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 652 ZCWPW1 peaks did not obviously overlap with DSB hotspots in Prdm9−/− mice.
source: However, it bears mentioning that we also detected 781 Zcwpw1 peaks in WT testes that did not obviously overlap with DSB hotspots and we detected 652 ZCWPW1 peaks that did not obviously overlap with DSB hotspots in Prdm9−/− mice (Figure 5B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 83.2% of the maintained ZCWPW1 peaks occurred within TSS ± 2 kb.
source: We analyzed these 781 ZCWPW1 binding sites in detail and we found that 83.2% of these maintained peaks occurred within TSS ± 2 kb, a substantially larger proportion than for the average position among all lost Zcwpw1 peaks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic feature analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The distribution pattern of H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 peaks overlapping with those 1,433 ZCWPW1 peaks was significantly different compared to the distribution pattern overlapping with DMC1-labelled DSB hotspots.
source: We also found that the distribution pattern of H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 peaks, which overlapped with those 1,433 ZCWPW1 peaks, was significantly different compared to the distribution pattern of H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 peaks that overlapped with DMC1-labelled DSB hotspots (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq signal distribution analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Zcwpw1 might have an additional transcription regulation function that is not obviously related to the Prdm9-mediated hotspot selection system.
source: Thus, although it is clear that the majority of the Zcwpw1 peaks resulted from Prdm9 activity, it is possible that Zcwpw1 might have an additional transcription regulation function that is not obviously related to the Prdm9-mediated hotspot selection system.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation of ZCWPW1 peaks at promoters that are independent of PRDM9.

claim: Prdm9 binds to specific DNA motifs in the genome and writes histone modifications (H3K4me3 and H3K36me3) via the methyltransferase activity of its PR/SET domain.
source: Our data support a working model wherein Prdm9 binds to specific DNA motifs in the genome and writes histone modifications (H3K4me3 and H3K36me3) via the methyltransferase activity of its PR/SET domain (Diagouraga et al., 2018; Powers et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' data and citations to prior work.

claim: PRDM9 binding leads to the recruitment of proteins required for the formation of DSBs in the vicinity of its binding site.
source: This leads to the recruitment of proteins required for the formation of DSBs in the vicinity of its binding site (e.g., SPO11, etc.) (Kumar et al., 2018; Panizza et al., 2011; Stanzione et al., 2016; Tessé et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on DSB formation.

claim: After Prdm9-catalyzed epigenetic modifications are deposited, Zcwpw1 can specifically read these H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks in the vicinity of DSB sites.
source: After these Prdm9-catalyzed epigenetic modifications are deposited, Zcwpw1 can specifically read these H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks in the vicinity of DSB sites, where Zcwpw1 functions to promote DSB repair; Zcwpw1 is not however required for DSB activity and localization (Mahgoub et al., 2019; Wells et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' data and citations to recent work.

claim: Zcwpw1 is not required for DSB activity and localization.
source: After these Prdm9-catalyzed epigenetic modifications are deposited, Zcwpw1 can specifically read these H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks in the vicinity of DSB sites, where Zcwpw1 functions to promote DSB repair; Zcwpw1 is not however required for DSB activity and localization (Mahgoub et al., 2019; Wells et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work by Mahgoub et al. and Wells et al.

claim: Zcwpw1's DSB-repair-promoting function greatly increases the overall completion rates of synapsis, crossover formation, and ultimately meiotic progression.
source: This DSB-repair-promoting function greatly increases the overall completion rates of synapsis, crossover formation, and ultimately meiotic progression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed defects in synapsis and crossover formation in Zcwpw1 mutants.

claim: Recombination hotspots are ubiquitous and active in all organisms.
source: The identification of recombination hotspots was first made in genetically-tractable experimental organisms such as bacteriophages and fungi, but it is now apparent that such hotspots are ubiquitous and active in all organisms (Wahls, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Higher-order chromosome architecture contributes to DSB hotspot localization.
source: Higher-order chromosome architecture, which can be described using the terminology of the 'tethered-loop/axis complex' model, contributes to DSB hotspot localization (Blat et al., 2002), and different strategies and mechanisms for the spatial regulation of DSB formation have evolved in different species, although these have many common features (Baudat et al., 2013; de Massy, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Different strategies and mechanisms for the spatial regulation of DSB formation have evolved in different species, although these have many common features.
source: Higher-order chromosome architecture, which can be described using the terminology of the 'tethered-loop/axis complex' model, contributes to DSB hotspot localization (Blat et al., 2002), and different strategies and mechanisms for the spatial regulation of DSB formation have evolved in different species, although these have many common features (Baudat et al., 2013; de Massy, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Spp1 promotes meiotic DSB formation by interacting with the axis-bound Spo11 accessory protein Mer2.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Spp1–whose PHD finger domain is known to read H3K4me3 marks– promotes meiotic DSB formation by interacting with the axis-bound Spo11 accessory protein Mer2 (Acquaviva et al., 2013; Sommermeyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on Spp1 in yeast.

claim: One or more other as-yet unknown proteins might function in a similar role to Spp1 during DSB formation in mammals.
source: Our study in mammals supports that one or more other as-yet unknown proteins might function in a similar role during DSB formation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that ZCWPW1 does not affect DSB formation.

claim: There is structural similarity between the zf-CW domain and the PHD finger of Spp1 that helps recognize histone H3 tails.
source: It is noteworthy that there is structural similarity between the zf-CW domain and the PHD finger of Spp1 that helps recognize histone H3 tails (Adams-Cioaba and Min, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior structural work.

claim: Deficiency of Zcwpw1 did not affect the recruitment of recombination-related factors like DMC1, MSH4, or RNF212.
source: However, somewhat surprisingly, our subsequent experiments indicated that deficiency of Zcwpw1 did not affect the recruitment of recombination-related factors like DMC1, MSH4, or RNF212, thereby implying that there might be other unknown proteins that function to link Prdm9 to meiotic recombination machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing normal recruitment of these factors in Zcwpw1 mutants.

claim: There might be other unknown proteins that function to link Prdm9 to meiotic recombination machinery.
source: However, somewhat surprisingly, our subsequent experiments indicated that deficiency of Zcwpw1 did not affect the recruitment of recombination-related factors like DMC1, MSH4, or RNF212, thereby implying that there might be other unknown proteins that function to link Prdm9 to meiotic recombination machinery.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that ZCWPW1 does not affect initial recombination factor recruitment.

claim: The PWWP domain has been shown to recognize H3K36me3 in both peptide and nucleosome contexts.
source: The zf-CW domain of ZCWPW1 has previously been shown to bind to H3K4me3 peptides (He et al., 2010), and the PWWP domain, another type of 'reader' module, has been shown to recognize H3K36me3 in both peptide and nucleosome contexts (Eidahl et al., 2013; Rondelet et al., 2016; Vezzoli et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior biochemical work.

claim: It is Prdm9's histone modification activity, rather than the chromatin residence of the Prdm9 protein per se, that might account for the functional interactions of the apparently co-involved Zcwpw1 and Prdm9 proteins.
source: One functional implication of our study is that it is Prdm9's histone modification activity, rather than the chromatin residence of the Prdm9 protein per se, that might account for the functional interactions of the apparently co-involved Zcwpw1 and Prdm9 proteins.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that ZCWPW1 binds to histone marks deposited by PRDM9 rather than to PRDM9 itself.

claim: Upon loss of the binding affinity of the Zcwpw1 zf-CW domain for H3K4me3 marks, the Zcwpw1 protein completely lost its ability to bind chromatin.
source: Our H3K4me3 reader-dead mutant mice showed that, upon loss of the binding affinity of the Zcwpw1 zf-CW domain for H3K4me3 marks, the Zcwpw1 protein completely lost its ability to bind chromatin, and spermatocytes in mice expressing this knock-in H3K4me3 reader-dead mutant Zcwpw1 exhibited a nearly complete failure of meiosis prophase I.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing no ZCWPW1 peaks in Zcwpw1KI/KI mice.

claim: Spermatocytes in mice expressing the knock-in H3K4me3 reader-dead mutant Zcwpw1 exhibited a nearly complete failure of meiosis prophase I.
source: Our H3K4me3 reader-dead mutant mice showed that, upon loss of the binding affinity of the Zcwpw1 zf-CW domain for H3K4me3 marks, the Zcwpw1 protein completely lost its ability to bind chromatin, and spermatocytes in mice expressing this knock-in H3K4me3 reader-dead mutant Zcwpw1 exhibited a nearly complete failure of meiosis prophase I.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and immunofluorescence data showing meiotic arrest in Zcwpw1KI/KI mice.

claim: ZCWPW1 is not required for DSB activity and localization.
source: Complementary analyses and similar conclusions were obtained by Maghoub et al and by Wells et al, establishing that ZCWPW1 is not required for DSB activity and localization (Mahgoub et al., 2019; Wells et al., 2019), findings which do not support the previous speculation that Zcwpw1 directs the location or the formation of DSBs (Li et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work by Mahgoub et al. and Wells et al.

claim: The findings do not support the previous speculation that Zcwpw1 directs the location or the formation of DSBs.
source: Complementary analyses and similar conclusions were obtained by Maghoub et al and by Wells et al, establishing that ZCWPW1 is not required for DSB activity and localization (Mahgoub et al., 2019; Wells et al., 2019), findings which do not support the previous speculation that Zcwpw1 directs the location or the formation of DSBs (Li et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' data and citations to recent work.
